chapter: Critics and the thinning Chicago scene (draft typing)
title: Teachers who stay a lesson ahead: music-store stories
summary: Hodes tells of a drum teacher giving a bass lesson. DeMichael adds his own story of being told to teach accordion. Hodes caps it with a school principal's tale of a clarinet teacher's note.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: A mother took her son into a music store for a bass lesson. It happened at noon, and the fellow at the desk hollered out to the back, hey, is there any bass player back there? Who's back there? And the guy answered, just me, I'm a drum teacher. Well, come on out here, you can give this guy a lesson. And he went out there and he gave him a lesson.

one of these places that went door to door, you rent the instrument and get so many lessons, then you can buy the instrument. At a big music store, I was complaining that I didn't have enough drum students. So the guy who was running the program said, well, you play vibes, why don't you teach accordion? I said, I don't play accordion. He says, you just stay a lesson ahead. I said, I can't do that. I can't do something like that.

Yeah. And the funniest experience was much later on, doing electric concert things in high schools. In Wisconsin, I did 88 one winter, in 1964. And I'm at one school and the principal after the concert was talking to me, I think he kind of liked my concert, he's getting kind of intimate, telling stories.

He says, I've got to tell you a story that happened here. He says, we have a teacher that teaches clarinet. And every lesson is, like, two dollars. And he does it in his room there, after school. And this one day he got a call from a hospital, his wife was in the hospital. And he had to rush
out. So he left a note on the music stand. Take the next page and leave your two dollars.
